Success
sŭk-sĕs´
n. (a prosperous outcome; the favourable issue of an undertaking)
From the Latin successus, an advance or good result. The word stands once in the KJV, in the charge given to Joshua at the Jordan, and it is tied there to a book rather than to a battle plan.

Biblical Definition

God commissions Joshua for a conquest and gives him one instrument: “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success” (Joshua 1:8). The chain is exact — the book in the mouth, meditation day and night, observance of what is written, and then prosperity and good success. Nothing is said about strategy or numbers. The command is repeated with its condition twice over: “Only be thou strong and very courageous, that thou mayest observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded thee: turn not from it to the right hand or to the left, that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest” (Joshua 1:7). The same doctrine opens the Psalter: “But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psalm 1:2), with its result, “And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper” (Psalm 1:3). Success in Scripture is the fruit of obedience to a revealed word, not an outcome pursued directly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines success as the favorable or prosperous termination of anything attempted; and good success as a prosperous issue.

expand to see more

SUCCESS, n. The favorable or prosperous termination of anything attempted; a termination which answers the purpose intended.

PROSPER, v.i. To be successful; to succeed; to be advanced in the pursuit of anything desirable.

MEDITATE, v.i. To dwell on anything in thought; to contemplate; to revolve in the mind.

LAW, n. In Scripture, the Mosaic institutions, or the revealed will of God; the rule of moral conduct.

OBSERVE, v.t. To keep religiously; to celebrate; to obey; to follow.

Key Scripture

Joshua 1:8 — "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success."

Joshua 1:7 — "Only be thou strong and very courageous, that thou mayest observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded thee: turn not from it to the right hand or to the left, that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest."

Psalm 1:2 — "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."

Psalm 1:3 — "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper."

Modern Corruption

Joshua 1:8 is detached from its object and used as a promise of career and financial advancement, so that a command about obeying a book becomes a technique for getting results.

expand to see more

No verse in the Old Testament is more regularly stripped of its terms than this one. The promise of good success is quoted, the conditions are dropped, and the whole is offered as an assurance that God will prosper the believer's plans. The verse says the opposite of what that use requires. The success promised is contingent on meditating in the law day and night and on observing to do all that is written therein, and the undertaking in view is the possession of Canaan under a divine mandate. A man may meet none of those conditions and quote the verse over a business.

The deeper corruption is in the definition of success itself. Prosperity teaching measures it by health, income and influence; Scripture measures it by whether a man did what God commanded. By the world's standard Jeremiah failed for forty years, our Lord failed at Calvary, and Stephen failed under the stones. Hebrews 11 lists men who subdued kingdoms and men who were sawn asunder in the same breath and calls both faith. The Reformed instinct here is the Westminster answer applied to vocation: the chief end is to glorify God and enjoy Him for ever, and any success that costs that end is failure with a good outcome attached.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sakal (H7919), to act wisely and so prosper; tsalach (H6743), to advance, prosper; hagah (H1897), to meditate, mutter; torah (H8451), law, instruction.

expand to see more

Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to be prudent, act wisely, have good success; Joshua 1:8.

Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to advance, prosper; make thy way prosperous.

Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to mutter, meditate; the day-and-night occupation with the book.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, direction; what must not depart out of the mouth.

Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, observe; that thou mayest observe to do.

Usage

"“Then thou shalt have good success” — the promise, with its conditions attached."

"“Turn not from it to the right hand or to the left” — the terms repeated."

"“Whatsoever he doeth shall prosper” — the Psalter's parallel."
